key_equations.explanation: Mu-hat is the cumulative treatment-effect estimate through batch T; tau-hat-t is the adjusted treatment-effect estimate for batch t; and v-hat-t is its estimated variance, so batches with smaller estimated variance receive greater weight.

narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical regret results use an idealized Beta-Bernoulli model; the guarantee for fractional rewards depends on an unobservable posterior approximation error and is less informative in dense-signal settings. The inferential guarantee is for the fixed-horizon estimate, so sequential peeking or early stopping invalidates the stated coverage. The comparison with ARMM and MADCovar is informationally asymmetric: those methods receive randomly preselected covariates, whereas DARTS learns from the full candidate pool.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The acquisition reward measures predictiveness of control outcomes, so it may not prioritize covariates that are chiefly useful for explaining treatment-effect heterogeneity or predicting treated outcomes. The evidence is based on simulations rather than real trials, and the reported computational burden—including about 35 CPU minutes per replication in the main method comparison—may limit practical use at larger scales.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose methods that account for dependence among covariates, including group LASSO rewards when covariate clusters are known and bandit methods with correlation structure. They also propose confidence-sequence inference to make the cumulative estimate valid for sequential monitoring and early stopping.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate DARTS in real experiments, including studies where covariate measurement costs and availability vary across participants or sites. Further work could also assess acquisition policies that target treatment-effect modifiers directly and compare methods under matched access to candidate covariates.

narrate.summary: This theory paper develops bounds on the covering radius of binary orthogonal arrays (OAs) with even strength. The objective is to bound how far any point in the binary space can be from its nearest array row. The authors improve linear programming (LP) bounds by using Krawtchouk polynomials and signed measures, with different bounds depending on whether farthest points have array rows at their antipodes. They also construct three infinite families of arrays related to BCH, Melas, and Zetterberg codes, and derive lower bounds using algebraic curves over finite fields. Their improved bounds are better than earlier bounds for non-tight arrays, and some examples have closely matching upper and lower bounds.
narrate.key_results: The new LP bounds improve on the Fazekas–Levenshtein bounds for non-tight arrays, subject to the paper’s stated cases concerning farthest points and their antipodes. For the first constructed family with length 15, the authors give a lower bound of 3 and an improved upper bound of 4, compared with the earlier upper bound of 5; at length 31, the lower bound is 10 and the improved upper bound is 11, compared with 12. For the Zetterberg-related family at length 17, the lower and upper bounds both equal 5, giving the exact covering radius; at length 65, the lower bound is 25 and the improved upper bound is 27, compared with the earlier upper bound of 28. The paper gives theoretical derivations and numerical comparisons for selected small lengths, rather than evaluating experimental designs on data.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that finding the exact covering radii of the three constructed families is a natural and difficult problem that remains open in general. They also note that obtaining analytical expressions for the cardinality-dependent bound is difficult when k is greater than 1.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The improved bounds rely on conditions about the farthest points, including whether their antipodes belong to the array; applying the strongest conditional bound may therefore require structural information that is not readily available. The numerical comparisons cover selected small lengths and constructed code families, so they do not establish performance across a broad range of arrays or real design settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify determining the exact covering radii of the three constructed families as an open direction. They also suggest that more detailed study of some examples could determine their exact radii.
narrate.future_work_unstated: It would be useful to develop practical procedures for identifying which conditional bound applies and for optimizing the cardinality-dependent bound at larger values of k. Further work could also assess these bounds for arrays with practical run constraints and test their usefulness in actual designed experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an adaptive discretization algorithm for locally optimal experimental design with constraints. It minimizes a convex design criterion, most often the D-criterion, while satisfying finite sets of convex inequality and affine equality constraints; a different design criterion can also be imposed as a constraint. The algorithm repeatedly optimizes the design on a finite set of candidate experiments, then adds an experiment that violates a sensitivity-based optimality condition. The authors prove convergence to an optimal design for the zero-tolerance version and finite termination at an approximately optimal design for the positive-tolerance version, under stated regularity and feasibility assumptions. Numerical examples use an exponential growth model and a chemical reaction-kinetics model, including constraints on average product return and measurement time.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves that the zero-tolerance algorithm either terminates at an optimal design or has accumulation points that are optimal, with criterion values converging monotonically to the optimum; its positive-tolerance version terminates finitely at a design meeting the specified optimality tolerance. In the exponential-growth examples, the algorithm required 2, 4, and 3 iterations, with reported runtimes of 0.1244, 0.2399, and 0.7182 seconds; the computed designs had 2, 4, and 3 support points. In the reaction-kinetics examples, the unconstrained and constrained designs each had 6 support points and required 8 and 9 iterations, with runtimes of 301.01 and 302.72 seconds; their reported approximation-error bounds were 2.6459 × 10⁻⁶ and 3.3856 × 10⁻⁵. The algorithm’s sensitivity-minimization subproblems have the dimension of the experiment space, compared with larger nonlinear subproblems in two of the cited methods, and the general version needs approximate global sensitivity minimization only when its preliminary search finds no violating experiment; these comparisons are analytical rather than head-to-head runtime tests.

key_equations.name: Discretization update

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the zero-tolerance version is not guaranteed to terminate after finitely many iterations. Its sensitivity minimization problem is generally nonconvex and may require computationally expensive global optimization. The convergence and termination results require regularity assumptions, including an initially strictly feasible discretized problem and a non-one-sidedness condition for the equality constraints.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstrations use finite candidate grids, so they do not establish how performance or design quality changes when the continuous experiment space is discretized differently. The reaction-kinetics examples take about 301 to 303 seconds even on the reported grid-based implementation, and the paper does not provide direct runtime comparisons against the cited algorithms on the same problems. The examples also use locally specified parameter values and a limited set of model types and constraints, leaving robustness to parameter uncertainty or model misspecification untested.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method against competing algorithms on shared constrained-design benchmarks, especially for very large candidate sets and continuous experiment spaces. Further work could also test robustness under parameter uncertainty and model misspecification, and extend the design formulation to practical restrictions such as exact run counts, replication limits, or sequential experiment selection.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a three-phase adaptive design for screening factors and optimizing a response within one experimental program. In the first phase, a modified definitive screening design and a screening statistic identify important factors and two-factor interactions using Elastic Net regression. In the second phase, the design adds experiments chosen according to the number and structure of the identified factors and interactions. In the third phase, a Gaussian process model guides optimization and selects six refinement runs in regions of high uncertainty. In simulations covering six scenarios, the method achieved 97.08% mean factor detection accuracy, with a mean prediction error of 3.61, while using an average of 41.5 runs.
narrate.key_results: Across six simulated scenarios and 540 evaluations, the method achieved 97.08% mean detection accuracy, compared with 83.33% for traditional sequential methods, 82.22% for augmented definitive screening designs, and 73.61% for standard definitive screening designs. The reported mean prediction error was 3.61, compared with 4.31 for traditional sequential methods; space-filling methods had lower errors, including 0.83 for Latin hypercube sampling and 1.45 for Sobol sequences, but provided no factor screening. The method maintained at least 90% detection accuracy in every scenario, including 90.0% in the interaction-heavy scenario. It used an average of 41.5 runs versus 29 for traditional sequential methods, a 43% increase, and the authors report statistically significant detection comparisons at below 0.001.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that validation used synthetic response functions and that industrial case studies are needed. The study focused on six continuous factors; higher dimensions, categorical factors, and mixture constraints need further investigation. They also note that Gaussian process computation may limit use when cumulative run counts are very large.

Prediction error is measured at the true optimum, so it does not by itself establish how well the method predicts across the response surface or how close the selected operating point comes to the optimum.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose industrial case studies, extension to higher-dimensional screening and categorical or mixed factors, and work on constrained and multi-response optimization. They also identify adaptive Bayesian sequential decision-making and an open-source software implementation as future directions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could report false-positive screening rates alongside detection accuracy and assess how threshold choices affect both measures. Testing the design under explicit blocking, restricted randomization, and practical run constraints would also clarify how readily it can be used in industrial experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper presents ALMAB-DC, a framework for sequential experimental design and optimization using a Gaussian process (GP) model and asynchronous parallel computing. It is intended for tasks such as response optimization, dose selection, and spatial sampling, with objectives including finding a high-performing setting and reducing prediction uncertainty. The method combines an acquisition rule, a multi-armed bandit (MAB) that allocates evaluations across regions, and a Kriging Believer (KB) update to diversify parallel proposals. Completed evaluations trigger new selections without waiting for every worker, using an event-driven dispatch rule. The authors report improved design performance over selected baselines and faster progress in wall-clock rounds, while noting that the results rely substantially on simulated evaluations.
narrate.key_results: In the polymer response-surface simulation, with 20 evaluations per run, ALMAB-DC using the upper confidence bound (UCB) had median final regret of 0.18% and an 85.4% success rate, compared with 0.41% and 78.0% for sequential Bayesian optimization. In the dose-response case, the reported median regret for the single-worker method was 0.00263; with four workers it reached zero within the same ten-round wall-clock budget. For spatial sampling, final integrated posterior variance (IPV) was 0.072 for ALMAB-DC and greedy maximum-variance selection, compared with 0.107 for Latin hypercube sampling and 0.098 for random selection; the rounds to reach the stated IPV threshold fell from 13 to 6 with two workers and to 4 with four. At four workers, asynchronous dispatch reached the stated thresholds in 7 versus 10 rounds for the response-surface case, 6 versus 8 for dose selection, and 4 versus 6 for spatial sampling; terminal regret was not statistically distinguishable from the synchronous versions in those comparisons.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces uMaxPro, a space-filling design method for computer experiments that aims to cover low-dimensional projections well while also avoiding bias in sampling the bounded design domain. It modifies the MaxPro criterion by replacing ordinary coordinate distances with periodic distances based on the minimum image convention. Designs are constructed as Latin hypercubes and optimized using simulated annealing with coordinate swaps. The authors compare the method with MaxPro and other sampling approaches using numerical integration, projection assessments, and structural engineering examples. They report that uMaxPro retains strong projection performance while producing statistically uniform samples and unbiased integration estimates.
narrate.key_results: Across 10,000 independent optimized designs, the authors report that MaxPro undersamples parts of the domain, with the reported undersampled volume reaching 34.77% in five dimensions; for uMaxPro, the reported value is 0.41%. In tests across two to five dimensions, uMaxPro has wrap-around discrepancy close to the Halton sequence, and its root mean square integration error decreases at a rate close to one divided by the number of points, with lower error than Halton on the tested interacting function. The integration comparisons use 500 independent runs and show biased estimates for MaxPro but unbiased estimates for uMaxPro. In engineering prediction tests averaged over 500 design realizations, uMaxPro performs well against the compared sampling methods; in the finite element concrete example, it improves estimation relative to MaxPro, while the paper notes that Halton can have a steeper error decrease at larger sample sizes.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a Bayesian optimal experimental design framework for identifying parameters in history-dependent constitutive models, with the goal of reducing parameter uncertainty. It uses expected information gain (EIG) to evaluate candidate experiments and derives a faster approximation based on the Fisher information matrix (FIM) and a Gaussian approximation to the posterior. To make optimization practical for batches of experiments, the authors train a neural-network surrogate of the FIM and reuse it across different batch sizes. Numerical studies design uniaxial tests for linear and nonlinear viscoelastic materials by choosing specimen hole geometry and loading paths, using simulated force and image data. The optimized designs generally improve parameter identifiability over random designs, including for parameters governing stress relaxation and other memory effects.
narrate.key_results: For linear viscoelasticity, the optimized single-test designs produced about 10% higher EGA utility than random designs and reduced average 95% credible-interval widths by 47% to 48%. Their marginal utility improvement was largest for stress-relaxation parameters, at 10.4% to 11.2%; the study also found a Spearman correlation of 0.67 between EGA utility and stress-state entropy. For nonlinear viscoelasticity, optimized batches improved utility by approximately 7% to 9% over random batches of the same size; average credible-interval reductions were 44% without loading-rate regularization and 29% with regularization. The FIM surrogates achieved over 97% mean relative accuracy for predicting the logarithm of the FIM and over 99.6% and 99.4% accuracy for approximate information gain in the linear and nonlinear studies, respectively. In the linear study, EGA evaluations were reported to cost four orders of magnitude less than the nested Monte Carlo comparison, which became impractical with the high-dimensional image data.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the Gaussian posterior approximation introduces bias in estimating expected information gain and can fail when the Fisher information matrix is singular or the likelihood is multimodal. They also note that their numerical studies focus primarily on uniaxial loading of planar specimens under simplified conditions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results come from simulated experiments rather than physical tests, so they do not establish that the selected geometries and loading paths deliver the same gains in a laboratory. The comparisons also rely on specified parameter priors, noise models, and a restricted family of planar specimens and loading controls, which may limit transfer to other materials or practical test constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using more general non-parametric posterior density estimation to reduce approximation bias and to incorporate nuisance uncertainty, such as uncertain boundary and initial conditions. They also propose extending the work to complex three-dimensional geometries and loading scenarios, with joint optimization of specimen topology and multiaxial protocols and possible use of three-dimensional volumetric data.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the predicted gains in physical material tests and compare posterior calibration with measured estimation error. Further work could also incorporate practical equipment limits and material variability directly into the design constraints, and assess whether the batch framework can be extended to adaptive, sequential testing.

narrate.summary: The paper applies the Taguchi method to optimize nonlinear pulse propagation in optical fibers. It uses balanced orthogonal arrays to choose simulation runs, scores each run with a response function, and updates factor settings and search intervals over repeated iterations. The authors test the approach on a guiding center soliton problem and on soliton-order conservation in a dispersion-decreasing fiber. In the latter case, a fractional factorial design uses nine runs for four factors at three levels, rather than the 81 runs of a full factorial design. Both simulations produce solutions close to the targeted pulse behavior, and the authors report rapid convergence in the guiding center example.
narrate.key_results: For the guiding center problem, the two-factor, three-level design uses nine runs per iteration; with a reduction rate of 0.8, the method converges in about 20 iterations, or 180 simulation runs. With the target soliton order set to 1.3285, it converges close to the theoretical gain of 3.5556 and launch power of 12.87 milliwatts. For the dispersion-decreasing fiber, the strength-two orthogonal array uses nine runs instead of the 81-run full factorial design, a nine-fold reduction; the study reports 450 simulation runs over 50 iterations. The resulting pulse width is within 10 femtoseconds of the target over 10 kilometers at a reduction rate of 0.9. In a supplementary comparison on the guiding center problem, the Taguchi method reaches the minimum objective in about 30 iterations, compared with about 50 for the genetic algorithm, while particle swarm optimization converges more slowly in the plotted comparison.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the designs in physical fiber experiments and assess sensitivity to measurement variation and realistic manufacturing or operating constraints. narrate.summary: This paper develops space-filling lattice designs for computer experiments, with the aim of supporting accurate prediction while maintaining adequate separation between runs. It presents an explicit rank-1 lattice construction based on algebraic numbers and a Korobov lattice construction that searches for a parameter using the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovasz basis reduction algorithm. The explicit construction determines its run sizes from the chosen algebraic parameters, while the Korobov construction can target a chosen prime run size. The authors prove that both approaches generate quasi-uniform families, balancing coverage and point separation. Their numerical results show that the lattice designs maintain the optimal separation-radius rate and can improve Gaussian process regression performance in lower dimensions.
narrate.key_results: The theory establishes that both constructions have covering and separation radii of order N to the power minus one over d; the explicit construction also has isotropic discrepancy of order N to the power minus one over d. In tested dimensions 2, 3, 5, and 7, the proposed lattices showed this optimal separation-rate behavior, unlike the compared random, Halton, and Sobol’ point sets, whose separation radii decayed faster. The Korobov construction generally had lower and more stable theoretical mesh-ratio bounds than the explicit construction; its search checks N minus 1 candidate parameters and has cost polynomial in dimension and quasi-linear in run size. In Gaussian process regression tests repeated over 100 noise realizations, both lattice designs generally performed better for sufficiently large run sizes in dimension 2 and had smaller asymptotic mean errors in dimension 3; no distinct prediction advantage appeared in dimensions 5 and 7 over the tested range.

key_equations.explanation: The covering radius h and separation radius q both have order N to the power minus one over d, where N is the number of points and d is the dimension.

key_equations.name: Korobov lattice generating vector

narrate.limitations_stated: The explicit construction does not allow arbitrary run sizes: its run sizes are determined by the Diophantine properties of its chosen algebraic parameters. The authors also note that the high-dimensional prediction comparisons are limited to a pre-asymptotic range by the computational cost of fitting Gaussian process models. Fixed algebraic parameters can produce poor low-dimensional projections, including overlaps or alignments that caused prediction-error spikes in one five-dimensional test.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The prediction comparison uses a limited set of synthetic benchmark functions and a single fixed Matérn smoothness setting, so the results do not establish performance for a broad range of real simulator responses or kernel choices. The Korobov search examines every candidate parameter, which may become burdensome at run sizes beyond those tested, and the evaluation does not compare against a broad range of established optimized space-filling designs.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose optimizing the algebraic parameter vector to improve the quality of low-dimensional projections and avoid structural anomalies in the explicit construction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate both constructions under practical input constraints, such as restricted factors or nonrectangular feasible regions, and compare them with optimized classical designs on real computer experiments. It could also investigate sequential ways to add runs while retaining the space-filling and separation properties.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a two-stage framework for estimating treatment effects in social A/B experiments where interactions between users can cause treatment effects to spill into the control group. Before the experiment, it constructs a weighted graph from multiple social behaviors and uses Balanced Louvain clustering to form clusters with fewer cross-cluster connections and controlled sizes. It then assigns clusters to treatment or control and adjusts bucket-level outcomes using pre-experiment predictions through CUPAC. The authors evaluate the approach in simulations and on Kuaishou’s social-sharing experiments. They report less spillover contamination and more sensitive treatment-effect estimates than with user-level randomization and standard variance-reduction comparisons.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, cluster-based assignment at a Within-Group Share Ratio near 0.95 reduced estimation bias by 87–89% compared with user-level randomization near 0.50; the paper reports that extrapolating to a ratio of 1.0 recovered the true effect within 0.1%. In an online comparison using a 2% sample of Kuaishou users, the ratio was 90.39% with cluster-based randomization and 49.68% with user-level randomization; reported treatment lifts were +26.612% versus +7.758% for share count, +14.774% versus +4.968% for share penetration, and +4.983% versus +1.888% for message penetration. The clustering partitioned approximately 370 million users into 73,340 clusters, with 44.7% of sharing events occurring within clusters. In a city-level clustering comparison, the combined soft and hard size constraints scored 0.716 on the paper’s composite criterion, compared with 0.631 for constrained label propagation and 0.294 for standard Louvain at resolution 1; its reported variance was 374,000, compared with 388,000 for Louvain at resolution 2. For seven-day retention, CUPAC reduced variance by 92.45% for the main-app metric and 93.77% for the combined-app metric, compared with 85.95% and 89.11% for CUPED.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that cluster-level assignment reduces the effective number of randomization units and can inflate variance. They also describe a trade-off: stronger size constraints can reduce modularity or within-cluster connectivity, and bucket-level prediction can inflate false-positive rates if overfitting is not controlled.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-world comparison is for a sharing strategy on one platform, so the results do not establish performance for other network structures, products, or treatment types. The paper reports cluster counts and maximum sizes but gives limited detail about the practical consequences of assigning clusters of unequal sizes or about how often clusters must be rebuilt as the graph changes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing dynamic network-aware randomization that adapts to changing interaction graphs. They also propose hierarchical clustering to support different business scenarios across social applications.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could test the method across more platforms, network structures, and treatment strategies, and compare its estimates with designs that directly model interference. It would also be useful to study operational constraints such as traffic limits, cluster reassignment over time, and sequential experiment use.

narrate.summary: The paper applies design of experiments (DoE) principles to trials of therapist-delivered interventions, with the aim of estimating intervention effects separately from therapist variation. It focuses on crossed designs, where each therapist delivers each intervention, and proposes randomising therapist–intervention combinations to patients. The authors develop completely randomised, batch-blocked, and multicentre batch-blocked factorial designs, with equal replication and blocking used to accommodate time and centre. They describe analyses using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and regression, including methods for testing intervention effects when blocking creates dependent random effects. Simulations support the proposed randomisation approach for estimating intervention and therapist effects, while also showing risks from some alternative allocation procedures.
narrate.key_results: The illustrative designs used 320 patients for the completely randomised and single-centre blocked cases, and 960 patients for the multicentre blocked case; these are examples, not optimised run sizes. The simulation study generated 10,000 datasets for each illustrative example and comparison, and generally estimated the intervention effect without bias across the five allocation methods. The estimated Type I error was 0.05 in most reported conditions, but was inflated when therapists were allocated after intervention assignment in a way that created an unadjusted patient-covariate imbalance. When therapists were not randomly allocated and allocation was associated with a prognostic patient characteristic, the estimated between-therapist variance rose from about 0.1 to around 1.0; randomising therapists to patients kept it near 0.1. The study does not report a general efficiency ranking or an optimal sample size; its comparisons concern estimation, standard errors, variance components, and error rates under selected simulated settings.

narrate.summary: The paper studies extremal orthogonal arrays (OAs), which are arrays with strength 2s minus 1 and exactly s distinct distances between rows. It treats them as designs in Hamming association schemes, a mathematical framework that organizes pairs by their Hamming distance. The authors construct a finer association scheme by separating rows according to one coordinate and distinguishing distances within and between the resulting groups. They prove that this construction has 2s minus 1 classes for tight designs and 2s classes otherwise. They also derive bounds on sums of distances and use the scheme construction to obtain a necessary condition for certain tight strength-three designs.
narrate.key_results: The constructed finer scheme has 2s minus 1 classes for tight extremal designs and 2s classes for nontight ones. For a tight strength-three design in H(q + 2, q), the paper shows that if q is greater than 2, q must be a multiple of four. The authors give a two-sided bound on the sum of the values obtained by subtracting each row distance from n; equality on the lower side occurs when the smallest value is zero, and equality on the upper side occurs for a tight design of strength 2s. The bound is attained in examples with the extended ternary Golay code in H(12, 3), where the sum is 9, and the ternary Golay code in H(11, 3), where the sum is 7. This is theoretical work and does not report efficiency comparisons or empirical run-size savings.

narrate.summary: This paper assesses whether large language models (LLMs) can construct useful two-level fractional factorial designs. It tests GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.5 Flash on designs with 8, 16, or 32 runs and varying numbers of factors, seeking designs with high resolution and minimum aberration. The authors create a zero-shot prompt that specifies the design objective and requests a design table in a fixed format, then evaluate repeated outputs against known best designs. Gemini performs especially well on selected small-factor tasks, while both models are unreliable on many larger or more complex tasks. The authors recommend established design references and software when the tested models do not perform consistently.
narrate.key_results: The study covered 36 tasks, with 10 independent executions per task for each model, producing 360 design outputs per model. Gemini 2.5 Flash found the minimum-aberration designs in all 10 executions for the 8-run tasks with 4 to 7 factors and for the 32-run task with 6 factors. For 16-run designs with 5 to 8 factors, Gemini found the minimum-aberration design in at least 8 of 10 executions; the paper reports that success for other design sizes was 50% or less. GPT-5.1 also found optimal 8-run designs, but less consistently, and found minimum-aberration 16-run designs with 5 to 8 factors in at least 8 executions except that it did not find the 12-factor optimum; its performance on larger 32-run tasks was generally weak.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that the tested models do not consistently construct attractive designs with larger numbers of factors, and advise using textbooks or established statistical software in those cases. Their conclusions concern the default model versions available when the study was conducted.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The comparison includes only two model versions and 36 specified tasks, so it does not establish how well other models or factor-and-run combinations would perform. The evaluation is based on generated design tables rather than response data or actual experiments, and some outputs required manual format correction before evaluation.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose testing few-shot prompts with carefully written chain-of-thought examples and retrieval-augmented generation using domain-specific design-of-experiments sources. They also encourage applying the task set as a benchmark for newer versions and other language models.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future evaluations could include more model families and repeated testing across model updates, while reporting generation cost and time alongside design quality and compliance. It would also be useful to test practical constraints, such as restricted factor combinations or follow-up runs, and validate whether model-generated designs support the intended estimates in real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper studies two-level supersaturated designs for screening many factors with relatively few runs. It extends Wu’s construction method, which starts with an orthogonal array (OA) and adds selected two-factor interaction columns that are partially aliased rather than fully aliased. The authors use J-characteristics to calculate the contributions of those columns to the E(s²) criterion, which measures average squared non-diagonal cross-products. They prove that designs containing all two-factor interactions are E(s²)-optimal when the starting array has one, two, or three fewer columns than runs. They also establish results for designs that omit a column, use only interactions, or restrict interactions to one parent factor.
narrate.key_results: When all two-factor interactions are added, the designs reach the theoretical E(s²) lower bound for starting arrays with one, two, and three fewer columns than runs; the reported values are n squared divided by n plus 1, n times n minus 4 divided by n minus 3, and n squared times n minus 5 divided by the product of n minus 3 and n minus 1, respectively. Omitting one column preserves optimality for the cases with one or two fewer starting-array columns. Using only interactions gives optimal designs in the first two cases; in the case with three fewer columns, the difference from the lower bound is reported as 8n(n minus 8) divided by the product of n minus 2, n minus 3, n minus 4, and n minus 5, and tends to zero as n increases. Restricting interactions to one parent factor is optimal when the starting array has one fewer column than runs, but is not optimal in the cases with two or three fewer columns.

key_equations.explanation: Here E(s²) is the average squared non-diagonal cross-product, m is the number of design columns, S is a set of three or four starting-array columns, and J₃(S) and J₄(S) are their third- and fourth-order J-characteristics.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that their methodology could be applied to starting arrays with fewer than three fewer columns than runs, but additional results for the corresponding J-characteristics would first be needed.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results are theoretical and are not validated through an applied experiment or comparison using observed responses. The constructions rely on particular orthogonal-array structures, and the paper does not assess whether their run layouts are practical under constraints such as restricted randomization or difficult-to-change factors.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the analysis to starting designs with fewer columns by establishing the additional J-characteristic results that would be required.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future research could evaluate these designs in real screening studies and examine how blocking, restricted randomization, or other practical run constraints affect their optimality. It could also study sequential use or alternative model and design criteria beyond the first-order screening model and E(s²).

narrate.summary: The paper develops a framework for using sample splitting to evaluate analysis methods and launch rules in A/B testing when the true impact of each test is unknown. It applies the method to per-test impact estimates assumed to be unbiased and normally distributed, with known sampling variances. Each test is partitioned so that one split applies the method and a separate split supplies an independent estimate of the true impact. The authors derive estimators and asymptotic confidence intervals for average performance, and examine choices of split fraction and number of partitions. Their theory and simulations show that sample splitting estimates performance on the split rather than full-test performance, creating a bias and variance tradeoff.
narrate.key_results: The authors show that average performance estimates are unbiased for the sample-split target, and derive asymptotic normality and valid confidence intervals as the number of tests grows. In simulations with 5K tests, the estimates had negligible bias for the sample-split target and the 95 percent confidence intervals covered it approximately 95 percent of the time. The simulations used 30 partitions as their benchmark and found minimal additional variance reduction beyond 30; increasing the number of independent tests consistently reduced variance. Allocating more than half the data to the methodology split reduced bias for full-test performance, but could increase variance; the mean-squared error optimum depended on the comparison being evaluated. For plug-in methods, resampling split estimates from their conditional distribution avoids repeated unit-level partitioning and, according to the authors, can reduce computational costs by orders of magnitude.

key_equations.name: Assumed impact-estimate model
key_equations.explanation: The estimated impact for test i, conditional on its true impact δᵢ, follows a normal distribution with mean δᵢ and sampling variance τᵢ².

key_equations.name: Sample-split performance target
key_equations.explanation: The target θ is the expected score p when methodology κ is applied to training-split data Xᵢa, with split fraction α and true impact δᵢ.

key_equations.name: Unbiased squared-error score
key_equations.explanation: The estimated score Ŷᵢs for partition s is the squared difference between the methodology output and the split-b impact estimate, minus the sampling variance of that estimate.

key_equations.name: Asymptotic distribution of average performance
key_equations.explanation: As the number of tests I grows, the estimated average performance θ-hat, centered at θ and scaled by the square root of I, approaches a normal distribution with mean zero and variance ζ².

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that sample-split estimates are generally biased for performance on the full sample because the methodology is applied to only part of the data. Their asymptotic inference may be unreliable with a small number of tests; they caution that confidence-interval coverage can be poor in that setting.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The framework relies on unbiased, normally distributed impact estimates with known variances and on tests being independent and identically distributed, assumptions that may not fit every testing system. The empirical validation is simulation-based and focuses on two specific comparisons, so it does not establish performance across real experiments, other methodology classes, or a broad range of performance measures.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the approach on historical or prospective experiments where the normality and known-variance assumptions are less plausible, and evaluate methods that change how impact estimates are constructed. It would also be useful to assess split choices under practical allocation constraints and to compare additional performance objectives beyond the examples studied here.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces Hyperparameter-Informed Predictive Exploration (HIPE), an adaptive method for choosing initial experiment batches in Bayesian optimization and active learning. It is designed for Gaussian process models and aims to reduce uncertainty in predictions while also learning the model hyperparameters that affect later optimization. HIPE combines Expected Predictive Information Gain, which targets predictive uncertainty, with Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement, which targets information about hyperparameters. The authors construct a batch criterion whose balance weight is determined by the information hyperparameters provide about test-point predictions, and optimize the criterion jointly over candidate batches. In the reported benchmarks, HIPE generally improves the balance of predictive accuracy, model calibration, and subsequent optimization performance, particularly when only a few large batches are available.
narrate.key_results: In batch active learning, using batches of 16 points for 4 rounds across 100 seeds, HIPE was the only method that consistently ranked among the top two for both predictive error and predictive calibration across the tested tasks. In two-batch optimization experiments with batches of 24 points, HIPE matched or exceeded the best method on the noisy synthetic benchmarks; on five benchmark optimization tasks tested across 200 seeds each, it had the highest final performance on four and was competitive on the fifth. On the 40-dimensional support vector machine task, HIPE achieved the highest optimization performance, narrowly ahead of the alternatives, and identified the two important input dimensions more effectively than space-filling initialization. In a reported 4-batch runtime comparison with batches of 8 points, HIPE acquisition optimization took 19.61 seconds, compared with 8.62 seconds for negative integrated posterior variance; initial model fitting took 21.91 seconds and model fitting during the optimization loop took 181.79 seconds for HIPE.

key_equations.name: Combined predictive and hyperparameter information criterion
key_equations.explanation: HIPE is the proposed batch criterion; X is the candidate batch; EPIG is Expected Predictive Information Gain under test-point distribution p*; BALD is Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement; and β is the weight balancing the two terms.

key_equations.name: Information-based balancing weight
key_equations.explanation: β is the balancing weight; I is mutual information; y(x*) is the response at test input x*; θ denotes model hyperparameters; D is the data already collected; x* is drawn from test-point distribution p*.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that HIPE can be computationally expensive, especially for large batches in higher dimensions. The paper focuses on Gaussian process surrogates; applying the method to other Bayesian models requires deriving a suitable acquisition function for those models.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical study relies on synthetic functions and benchmark or surrogate tasks, rather than reporting validation in a physical or operational experiment. Most optimization comparisons use only two batches, so the results provide limited evidence about performance over longer sequential campaigns or under practical constraints on which input combinations can be tested.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending HIPE to transfer learning, including use with a multi-task Gaussian process and data from related problems. They also propose incorporating expert knowledge through a non-uniform test-point distribution and studying multi-objective settings with multiple surrogates that share input locations.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test HIPE in real experiments and assess how it performs when inputs have operational restrictions, such as discrete choices, forbidden combinations, or limited resources. It would also be useful to study cheaper approximations for large batches and repeated sequential use when observations arrive over many rounds.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces mutual transport dependence (MTD), a geometric criterion for optimal experimental design that aims to select experiments useful for estimating an unknown quantity. Unlike mutual information (MI), the MTD compares the joint distribution of the unknown quantity and the outcome with the product of their marginal distributions using optimal transport. Its transport cost can be chosen to reflect the parameter scale, a transformed representation, or a task-specific priority. The authors estimate the criterion from samples and optimize designs with gradient-based methods when the experiment simulator is differentiable. In simulated benchmarks, the method often gives lower parameter-estimation errors than the MI-based comparison and can be tailored to prioritize a specified decision.
narrate.key_results: For the Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) benchmark after 10 sequential experiments, MTD had lower reported root mean squared errors than posterior contrastive estimation (PCE) across all reported parameter metrics; for example, error for rho was 0.018 with MTD versus 0.047 with PCE, and error for alpha was 0.009 versus 0.036. In source location finding over 25 experiments, MTD produced lower error through most of the rollout, although the MI-based designs had similar error by the final iteration. In that location-finding comparison, optimizing one design took about 30 seconds for MTD and about 120 seconds for PCE under the reported implementation. A weighted transport cost reduced the reported zero-one loss more quickly when the task included identifying whether a source was in a specified region.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for deciding both which experiment to run next and when to stop a sequential campaign. It frames sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) as a finite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP), with expected information gain (EIG) balanced against experimental cost. The stopping decision compares the reward from stopping now with the expected value of continuing, while a policy-gradient method learns continuous design choices. A training curriculum gradually shifts from forced continuation to the learned stopping rule to reduce premature stopping during learning. Simulations show that the approach can learn cost-aware design and stopping policies, with the clearest benefit when earlier design choices affect later experimental opportunities.
narrate.key_results: In the linear-Gaussian benchmark, the analytical best utilities were 2.892 for four experiments at zero cost, 1.703 for one experiment at cost −0.5 per experiment, and 2.047 for two experiments at cost −0.25 per experiment. The tested maximum horizons were 3, 4, and 5 experiments; at zero cost the learned policy continued to the allowed maximum, while at negative costs it learned earlier termination. In the source-detection example with a cost of −0.5 per experiment and maximum horizon 4, vanilla training settled at an average stopping stage of about 2.4, while curriculum training stopped slightly after stage 3 and attained substantially higher reward. On one illustrative source-detection trajectory, the vanilla policy stopped after two experiments and earned −0.564, whereas the curriculum-trained policy continued for three experiments and earned 2.198. The source-model surrogate had test mean-squared error on the order of 10⁻⁶ and was approximately 10⁵ times faster than the numerical solver.

key_equations.name: Value-based stopping rule
key_equations.explanation: Here s is the current state, r_T(s) is the immediate reward for stopping there, Q(s) is the expected value of continuing with another experiment, and the comparison means stop when the immediate reward is no smaller.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that evaluating rewards can be costly when posterior updates or Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence calculations are expensive, especially for high-dimensional parameters. They also note a circular dependence between the learned continuation value and the training data distribution, and that the paper focuses on information gain rather than other scientific objectives.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulations rather than real experimental campaigns, so practical performance under real measurement noise, logistics, or operational constraints is not demonstrated. The examples use short maximum horizons of 3 to 5 experiments and selected model settings; the paper does not establish how results scale to longer campaigns or compare performance across a broad set of methods and repeated real-world studies.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose combining the framework with scalable posterior approximations, amortized inference, or surrogate models for information gain. They also suggest direct stopping-policy parameterizations or offline pretraining of continuation values to improve robustness, and extending the objective to predictive performance or other task-specific scientific goals.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the learned policies in real experiments and test them under practical constraints such as hard budgets, safety limits, and unavailable or costly design settings. Further work could also assess transfer to longer campaigns and sequential retraining as new data arrive, and provide reusable software and reproducible benchmarks.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for choosing the path of a moving sensor to reduce uncertainty in a Bayesian inverse problem governed by a linear partial differential equation (PDE). The sensor makes continuous or frequent measurements of the evolving state, and the unknown parameters have a Gaussian prior while measurement errors have a Gaussian noise model. The authors derive the posterior covariance as a function of the path, then optimize trace-based or determinant-based uncertainty criteria while enforcing path and control constraints. They represent feasible paths through an ordinary differential equation for sensor motion and use a time discretization designed to remain consistent as it is refined. Simulations of pollutant transport show that optimized paths can reduce posterior uncertainty, and that coarser solutions can provide useful starting points for finer optimization.
narrate.key_results: In the two-parameter pollutant example, the A-optimal utility fell from 0.791 to 0.493 for initial path 1, and from 1.149 to 0.729 for initial path 3; path 2 instead rose from 1.090 to 1.119. For path 1, refining the sensor time step through six halvings to about 1.5 × 10^-4 led to an optimization that reached the reported optimum in one iteration, using two objective and two gradient evaluations. In the 25-dimensional parameter-reduced example, the reduced space captured 99.01% of prior sample energy, and optimization lowered the A-optimal utility from 6.359 × 10^-3 to 5.461 × 10^-3, a relative factor of 0.859, in 184 seconds. The study compares starting paths and measurement setups within its simulation, rather than benchmarking against other design algorithms; source code and data are reported as publicly available.

key_equations.name: Posterior covariance for a sensor path
key_equations.explanation: The posterior covariance Σpost for path p is computed from the measurement map G, the noise covariance Σnoise, and the prior covariance Σpr; the superscript T denotes matrix transpose.

key_equations.name: A-optimal and D-optimal design criteria
key_equations.explanation: The A-optimal utility ΨA is the trace of the posterior covariance, and the D-optimal utility ΨD is its determinant; the design seeks a path that minimizes the selected utility.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors restrict the main formulation to linear parameter-to-observable maps and a single moving sensor. Their parameter-field example uses a 25-dimensional parameter-reduced posterior, and they state that an efficient, scalable extension to parameter fields remains future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is limited to simulated pollutant transport in one domain, so performance with real sensor data, model error, or different environmental systems is not established. The objective is non-convex and the reported outcomes depend on initial paths; the paper does not establish global optimality or compare the method broadly with alternative design algorithms. Fine time discretizations also make gradient calculations costly, and the high-dimensional result depends on a specific prior-based reduction.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the design criteria, including expected information gain, to nonlinear parameter-to-observable maps, and developing scalable approaches for infinite-dimensional parameter fields using model reduction and multifidelity techniques. They also propose improving robustness to aleatoric uncertainty and finding cheaper ways to generate initial paths; they note that extending the approach to multiple sensors is straightforward.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be validation with a physical mobile-sensing experiment, including measured navigation error and noise-model calibration. It would also be valuable to evaluate practical operational constraints such as battery limits, communication loss, and restricted flight corridors, and to assess whether the optimized paths remain effective when those constraints or the transport model are imperfect.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for removing candidate points that cannot belong to any optimal exact design without changing the best achievable design. It addresses finite candidate sets and the D-optimality objective for estimating model parameters. The method uses an optimal approximate design and a known nonsingular exact design to screen candidates with an augmentation condition, followed by a more computationally involved exchange condition. The authors apply the screening before exact-design optimization using mixed-integer second-order cone programming. Their examples show that this preprocessing can shrink very large candidate sets enough to make exact-design computation feasible, while the paper also proves that sufficiently large designs have support within a maximum-variance set.
narrate.key_results: In simulated Gaussian-regressor examples with candidate sets from 10^4 to 10^8 points, the augmentation screen reduced the sets to about 100 or fewer candidates; the exchange screen gave moderate additional reduction in this model class. In the constrained mixture example, screening reduced 9,991 candidates to 1,644 after augmentation and then to 390 after exchange. For the mixture problem, the exact-design solver was stopped after 60 seconds with a reported gap of 0.87%; the returned design had a D-criterion value of 1.495 × 10^-4, compared with 1.169 × 10^-4 for the previously reported design. For the discretization with 981,901 candidates, the authors report that exchange screening reduced the remaining set by more than a factor of ten beyond augmentation, with the number retained depending non-monotonically on design size.

key_equations.name: Information matrix
key_equations.explanation: The information matrix M for design w is the sum over candidate indices i from 1 to N of each weight w_i times the regressor vector f_i and its transpose.

key_equations.name: D-optimality criterion
key_equations.explanation: The criterion Phi of information matrix M is its determinant raised to the reciprocal of m, the number of model parameters.

key_equations.name: Augmentation screening condition
key_equations.explanation: For candidate index ell to be eligible for an optimal exact design, its optimal-approximate-design variance value v_ell star must be at least m times n times the difference between the efficiency of the known exact design w_n_plus and the quantity n minus 1 divided by n.

key_equations.name: Single-point exchange condition

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that candidate reduction is impossible in certain highly symmetric models where criterion-preserving transformations map any candidate to any other, so every candidate supports some optimal exact design. narrate.limitations_unstated: The method depends on having an optimal approximate design and a nonsingular exact design available; the paper's practical results therefore do not establish equal performance when either input is difficult to obtain. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to multivariate responses and to exact designs with additional constraints. They also propose developing candidate-removal methods for other criteria, particularly A-optimality, and studying the computational complexity of determining the set of candidates that support optimal exact designs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test screening under errors in the approximate-design calculation and establish safe numerical tolerances for candidate elimination. It could also evaluate the method on a broader range of industrial experiments and incorporate practical restrictions such as costs, blocking, or forbidden run combinations.

narrate.summary: This review introduces Bayesian optimization as a way to choose experiments iteratively when the objective is costly to measure and its functional form is unknown. It is written for bioprocess engineering, including tasks such as optimizing reaction conditions, media, strains, and scale-up. The authors describe a workflow using initial experiments, a probabilistic surrogate model, an acquisition function to choose subsequent experiments, and a stopping rule. They give practical guidance on experimental coverage, model choices, measurement noise, batch effects, and calibration, alongside illustrative simulated examples. The review finds that methods accounting for biological and measurement complications can improve the guidance provided by the model, while also identifying barriers to wider use and areas needing further development.
narrate.key_results: In the illustrative simulated pH optimization, the paper reports that the procedure identifies the global optimum at pH 7.2 by iteration 6. The associated figure shows the model fitted to five initial data points; this is an example, not a general run-size result. In a separate simulated biocatalysis example, a hybrid model accounting for first-order reaction kinetics and batch effects learns more efficiently from seven observations per reaction than a naive Gaussian process model, although no numerical error or efficiency measure is reported. As practical guidance rather than a comparative finding, the authors suggest that initial experiments may use roughly half the total experiment budget and that an appropriate kernel length scale may be one-quarter to one-half of the parameter-space width.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that real-world use of Bayesian optimization in bioprocess engineering remains nascent and that more experience is needed to establish standards for selecting models, priors, and acquisition functions. They also note that some approaches are computationally demanding and that specialized algorithms are needed for complex parameter spaces.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The review does not report a systematic literature search or a reproducible method for selecting and evaluating the cited studies, so its guidance is not presented as a formal evidence synthesis. Its examples are illustrative simulations rather than prospective comparisons in real experimental campaigns, and it gives no shared quantitative benchmark for performance against conventional design of experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for domain scientists to test, evaluate, and further develop the recommendations, and for machine learning researchers to develop methods tailored to bioprocess challenges. They also identify the need for more user-friendly tools, reusable model components, and stronger practices for sharing data, software, and documentation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective, multi-site studies comparing the recommended approaches with conventional experimental designs under realistic budget, batch, and measurement constraints. Shared benchmarks could also test sensitivity to model misspecification and measurement drift, while reporting both optimization quality and the number and cost of experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes the data-pooling treatment roll-out (DPTR) framework to help online platforms decide which policies to deploy when each randomized experiment has limited data. It targets positive average treatment effects across multiple experiments and can also guide heterogeneous treatment effect decisions for groups within one experiment. The method combines each experiment's own effect estimate with the average estimate across experiments, using a data-driven scale to control shrinkage and applying the resulting lower decision bound to select policies. The authors analyze the method theoretically for non-overlapping linear experiments and evaluate other settings through simulations and real datasets. They find that pooling often improves deployment reward over individual treatment roll-out, especially with small samples and many experiments, while noting important limits under strong interactions and tight deployment capacity.
narrate.key_results: In simulations of non-overlapping linear experiments with covariates, for noise variance 9, the optimality ratio was 0.1003 for individual treatment roll-out, 0.7123 for DPTR with a shared scale, and 0.7612 for DPTR with personalized scales when there were 100 experiments; with 5 experiments, the corresponding values were 0.0990, 0.3726, and 0.5882. In a real overlapping-experiment dataset, DPTR exceeded individual treatment roll-out for every estimator and sample size reported: for the double machine learning estimator at sample size 1,000, the values were 0.3654 and 0.0080, respectively, and at sample size 20,000 they were 0.5474 and 0.2145. The paper's theory establishes weak improvement over the individual method in its analyzed setting and strict improvement under a positive pooled anchor as the number of experiments grows. In the Criteo subgroup analysis, which used 1,744 groups and repeatedly sampled 10 to 30 users per group, the authors report higher reward for DPTR than for individual roll-out at each tested sample size, alongside higher recall and lower specificity.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that formal guarantees cover non-overlapping experiments with linear specifications, while other settings are assessed empirically. narrate.limitations_unstated: The approach pools toward a single average anchor, which may be a poor match when experiments belong to distinct populations or have markedly different effect patterns; the paper does not establish a general rule for detecting when pooling should be restricted. The real-data evaluations use resampling and full-sample estimates as benchmarks rather than prospective deployment outcomes, so they do not directly measure realized business effects after rollout.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the approach to continuous treatments, observational data, and optimization problems with uncertain objectives. They also identify capacity-constrained deployment as requiring additional analysis.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to develop diagnostics or clustered anchors that identify which experiments are sufficiently comparable to pool, then assess those choices on new datasets. Prospective validation in live randomized rollouts, including checks for changes in effects over time, would clarify how well the estimated reward gains transfer to deployment.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an estimator and an adaptive assignment strategy for sequential experiments with binary treatment, focusing on estimating the average treatment effect. Its adaptive-design-likelihood-based targeted maximum likelihood estimator uses the average of the experiment's treatment assignment rules to update an outcome model, rather than relying on each unit's individual assignment probability. The authors show theoretically that this estimator is asymptotically normal and semiparametrically efficient under conditions requiring positivity and stabilization for the average assignment rule. They also propose an adaptive design that steers this overall average toward an estimated variance-minimizing Neyman allocation. Simulations find lower estimator variance for the proposed estimator than for the earlier adaptive-design estimator, and lower variance for the proposed assignment strategy than for standard Neyman adaptation.
narrate.key_results: The simulations used 5,000 Monte Carlo runs, a burn-in of 1,000 units, 250 additional units at each subsequent time point, and 10 time points. At time point 10 under standard Neyman allocation, the proposed estimator had reported variance of 2.03 × 10⁻², mean squared error of 2.04 × 10⁻², and 92.6% coverage for its 95% confidence interval; under the benefit-driven design, the corresponding values were 4.91 × 10⁻², 5.00 × 10⁻², and 94.2%. The paper reports that the proposed estimator had lower variance than the earlier estimator under both adaptive designs, and that the proposed average-design-driven strategy consistently had lower variance than standard Neyman adaptation and moved closer to the oracle design. The authors establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency theoretically, with the required positivity and stabilization conditions applying to the average assignment rule.

narrate.summary: The paper studies the multiplicative algorithm (MA) for optimal experimental design (OED), where a probability distribution over a finite set of design points is chosen to maximize an information-based criterion for parameter estimation. It gives an optimization-based proof that the algorithm's objective values do not decrease under conditions on a transformed version of the criterion and on the gradient at the current design. The proof uses a matrix Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and also yields sufficient conditions for strict improvement. Two examples show that the choice of the algorithm's power parameter can strongly affect behavior, and that zero gradient components can prevent the algorithm from continuing. The paper also discusses open questions about applying the algorithm to a generalized design formulation that permits estimation of parameter subsystems.
narrate.key_results: The monotonicity result applies when the transformed criterion is differentiable, isotonic, and concave, and the gradient is positive on the current design's support; it covers criteria including D-, A-, and certain pth-mean criteria. With a power parameter strictly between zero and one, the objective strictly increases whenever the current design is not unchanged, under the theorem's conditions. In a two-point, two-parameter A-criterion example, a power parameter of one causes cycling, while one-half reaches the optimum in one step; the example's objective-gap contraction factor is the absolute value of one minus twice the power parameter. In a three-point, three-parameter c-criterion example, a zero gradient component makes the next design have objective value minus infinity, so the algorithm cannot proceed. These are theoretical examples rather than empirical comparisons or run-size evaluations.

key_equations.name: Moment matrix and design objective
key_equations.explanation: The weight w_i for design point i multiplies its Fisher information matrix A_i; summing over n design points gives the moment matrix M(w), and the criterion ϕ evaluated at that matrix gives the objective f(w).

key_equations.name: Multiplicative update
key_equations.explanation: At iteration k, each weight w_i is multiplied by the corresponding gradient component raised to the power parameter lambda, then normalized by the sum over design points j to form the next weights.

key_equations.name: Transformed criterion
key_equations.explanation: The transformed criterion ψ at a positive definite matrix M is the negative of the original criterion ϕ evaluated at the inverse of M.

key_equations.name: Monotonicity guarantee
key_equations.explanation: Under the paper's assumptions on the transformed criterion and positivity of the gradient on the current design's support, the objective at iteration k plus one is at least the objective at iteration k.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that monotonicity does not by itself ensure convergence to an optimum when the original criterion is nonconcave. They also show that if gradient components are zero, as can occur for the c-criterion, the algorithm may leave the feasible region on which its objective is finite and fail to continue. For the generalized formulation, they leave open whether dropping coordinates preserves feasibility and monotonicity and whether an optimal solution has the dropped coordinates equal to zero.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The analysis is for a finite design space and locally specified information matrices, so its conclusions do not establish performance when the assumed statistical model or the locally chosen parameter value is inaccurate. The paper provides theoretical examples but no computational benchmarks, real-experiment validation, or assessment of the practical cost of reaching a useful solution on larger design problems.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating coordinate dropping for the generalized design formulation. They identify feasibility after a coordinate becomes zero, objective monotonicity across the support change, and existence of an optimal solution with that coordinate zero as open questions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test variants that handle zero gradient components and other practical constraints, then compare their performance with alternative design algorithms on representative finite design problems. Further analysis could also examine robustness to locally misspecified information matrices and validate the method in actual experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops sample size calculations for split-plot factorial longitudinal cluster-randomised trials with continuous outcomes. The method addresses a cluster-level treatment assigned through a longitudinal cluster-randomised design and an individual-level treatment assigned within cluster-periods. It derives treatment-effect variances for models that include or omit an interaction, and extends the calculations to unequal cluster-period sizes. The calculations combine the individual-treatment variance expressions with the variance for the corresponding single-factor longitudinal cluster trial. In an application to the SharES breast cancer trial, the required observations per cluster-period differed according to the assumed correlation structure and whether the model included an interaction.
narrate.key_results: For the SharES design, which had 25 clusters across six periods, targeting an effect size of 0.35 standard deviations with 80% power and a 0.05 significance level required 4 observations per cluster-period for the cluster-level effect and 2 for the individual-level effect without an interaction under an exchangeable correlation structure. With an interaction, the corresponding requirements were 6, 3, and 6 observations for the cluster-level effect, individual-level effect, and interaction; under the block-exchangeable structure these were 7, 3, and 5. Without an interaction, the block-exchangeable requirements were 5 observations for the cluster-level effect and 2 for the individual-level effect. At an effect size of 0.2, the block-exchangeable requirements for the cluster-level effect rose to 71 observations with an interaction and 61 without one, compared with 21 for either model under the exchangeable structure; the individual-level and interaction requirements were 11 and 21, respectively.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the method assumes continuous outcomes and either an exchangeable or nested exchangeable correlation structure. It also assumes block randomisation of the individual-level treatment, so that the treatment allocation proportion is fixed within each cluster-period.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The worked numerical evaluation focuses on one healthcare trial and a limited set of correlation assumptions, so it offers little evidence about performance across other longitudinal designs or practical allocation patterns. The calculations also depend on specified variance and correlation parameters, but the paper does not evaluate how errors in those inputs affect the resulting sample sizes.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to binary and time-to-event outcomes, to other within-cluster correlation structures such as decay structures, and to designs with more treatment factors. They also identify designs in which eligibility for one treatment depends on allocation to another as a direction for generalisation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess the accuracy of these sample size calculations through simulation across a broader range of longitudinal designs and parameter misspecification. Practical tools could also evaluate constrained allocation patterns and help trial teams compare designs using realistic recruitment and cluster-size information.

narrate.summary: The paper develops interleaved lattice-based maximin distance designs for mixed continuous, ordinal, and binary variables. The objective is to spread computer experiment runs through the input space by maximizing the minimum Euclidean distance between design points; no response model is specified. The design construction combines a lattice structure with choices of levels for each variable, then selects a translation to bring the number of runs close to the target. The authors provide separate construction algorithms for lower, middle, and higher numbers of variables. Their numerical comparisons show that the method often produces larger separation distances than existing methods for mixed-variable designs, while performing similarly to the continuous-variable method it extends when all variables are continuous.
narrate.key_results: For mixed continuous and ordinal inputs, the reported separation distances are typically two to ten times those from the constrained-design method of Stinstra and colleagues. For all-ordinal inputs, the new method generally outperforms the methods of Sun and colleagues and Stinstra and colleagues, although Stinstra’s method is sometimes equally good. For all-continuous inputs, the new method and the continuous-variable method of He have nearly identical separation distances in most cases, with occasional slight improvements by the new method. In one example with 3 variables and a target of 10 runs, the new design has separation distance 0.75, compared with 0.7071 for the continuous-variable design; another example obtains 62 runs with separation distance 0.3466.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a method for testing whether a new policy improves outcomes over a standard control in A/B experiments. It targets the average treatment effect and covers both independent observations and experiments with effects that carry over between time periods. The method constructs doubly robust pseudo-outcomes, applies an adaptive two-armed bandit rule to form test statistics, and combines results from randomly permuted sample orders. For dynamic experiments, it uses a reinforcement-learning estimator to construct pseudo-outcomes from daily trajectories. The authors report controlled type-I error and higher power than comparison tests in theoretical results, simulations, and evaluations using ridesharing data.
narrate.key_results: In the passenger-subsidy datasets, the permutation-based two-armed bandit test produced p-values of 0.482, 0.044, and 0.023; the corresponding bandit-only values were 0.571, 0.086, and 0.041, and the double machine learning values were 0.574, 0.055, and 0.027. The tests did not reject on the A/A dataset, while the permutation-based test and double machine learning test rejected at the 5% level on the other two datasets; the bandit-only test did not reject on the second dataset. In simulations with unconfounded and confounded treatment assignment, the authors report that the permutation-based test generally had the highest power among the proposed test, the bandit-only test, and double machine learning, while maintaining appropriate type-I error in most tested settings. For dynamic experiments, the study used 1,000 simulation replications; in real-data-based bootstrap environments, all three tests kept type-I error below the nominal 0.05 level, and the permutation-based test outperformed the bandit-only test in most scenarios. The paper also evaluated five ridesharing datasets in total, but the dispatch-policy power assessment used bootstrap-generated data based on two A/A datasets rather than a live randomized dispatch-policy experiment.
